scopeReview: CED Topic 1.3 LIM-1.C: one-/two-sided function limits read from original plotted graphs, including graph scale/domain care. All eleven questions include an actual local SVG diagram plus a detailed accessible description. No absent-image references, formal derivative calculations or BC-only concepts.
varietyReview: Graph types vary across holes, jumps, a sampled rising curve, continuous corners, endpoints, reflection, horizontal input shift and multiple candidate locations. Several require separating open/closed points and side direction; repeated hole/one-sided skills are intentional within this graph-reading topic, not merely parameter-swapped clones. All graphs are original coordinate constructions.
repetitionReview: Each prompt and all four options were read separately; distinct tasks/contexts within this set. Cross-topic exact duplicates checked by validator. Semantic similarity and AP difficulty remain judgment calls, not proven by an automated score.

questions.independentReasoning: The left segment ends and the right segment begins at exactly (2,5); their endpoint ordinates agree. The isolated dot at (2,−1) supplies only the point value. The plotted-segment solver separately reads both approach heights.
optionReview: This is the assigned value f(2), not the common approaching height.
This is the target input coordinate, not the limiting output.
The hollow point does not prevent a limit; both sides approach the same height.
Correct: both nearby branches approach height 5.

questions.independentReasoning: The plotted left segment rises from (−4,0) to (−1,3). Its equation near the endpoint is y=x+4, so its approaching height is 3 independently of the other plotted components.
optionReview: Correct: the branch followed from inputs smaller than −1 approaches height 3.
This is the right-hand approaching height, not the left-hand height.
This is the filled point’s height and therefore f(−1).
This is the input approached, not a limiting output.

questions.independentReasoning: Reading the endpoints from the original plotted line data gives ordered side values (1,−3). Their difference is 4 rather than zero. The independent segment routine therefore returns no common limit and checks exactly one matching choice.
optionReview: Averaging the two heights does not produce an approached value from either side.
Correct: the left- and right-hand limits are 1 and −3, which disagree.
This is the filled point’s height, not a common nearby height.
This describes only the right-hand approach and ignores the left branch.

questions.independentReasoning: The last point of the left polyline and first point of the right polyline both have coordinates (3,9). Their shared ordinate, not the isolated dot at y=2, determines the limit. No unplotted smoothness or exact parabola formula is assumed.
optionReview: This is the point value f(3), shown by the separate filled dot.
This is the input coordinate rather than the output height.
Correct: the rising branch approaches the missing height 9 from both directions.
An isolated missing point on an otherwise joined branch does not destroy its limit.

questions.independentReasoning: The right segment runs from (0,2) to (3,5), with local equation y=x+2. Inputs tending to zero from above therefore yield outputs tending to 2. The left endpoint at 7 is on the wrong side.
optionReview: This is the left-hand limit, whereas the plus sign requests the right-hand limit.
The filled dot gives f(0), not the requested one-sided limit.
The arithmetic mean of the side heights is irrelevant to a specified right-hand approach.
Correct: the branch for positive inputs approaches the right hollow endpoint at height 2.

questions.independentReasoning: The segment ending at x=1 and the segment beginning at x=1 each have endpoint ordinate −6. This is a function-value limit, not a derivative question, so different segment slopes create no ambiguity.
optionReview: Correct: both segments join at the same vertex height −6.
A change in slope does not require the function’s limiting value to be zero.
This is the vertex’s x-coordinate, not its y-coordinate.
A corner may have a well-defined function limit even though its slopes differ.

questions.independentReasoning: The left segment from (−5,1) to (−2,4) has slope 1 and approaches y=4 at −2. The independent model uses left-side segments only; it does not impose or invent any right-side graph.
optionReview: This is the assigned value at the endpoint.
Correct: the existing branch approaches height 4 from inputs less than −2.
This is the target input, not the approaching output.
A right branch is unnecessary for the explicitly requested left-hand limit.

questions.independentReasoning: The two plotted segments share the vertex y=2. Negating each side’s endpoint value gives (−2,−2), which agree. The graph-model check performs the output sign change before testing the actual options.
optionReview: This is the limit of f; the negative sign in g reverses its output.
This is the input location, not the reflected output.
Correct: f approaches 2 from both sides, so reflecting its outputs changes the approaching height to −2.
The corner does not prevent either f or its reflection from approaching a common height.

questions.independentReasoning: The first plotted segment has endpoints (2,−3) and (3,−2), so its local equation is y=x−5. Approaching x=2 from above gives −3. This avoids a convention-dependent claim about two-sided limits at domain endpoints.
optionReview: This is the endpoint’s input coordinate.
This changes the sign of the displayed endpoint height without justification.
A right-hand limit uses the existing right branch; no left-side domain values are needed.
Correct: the available right branch approaches the endpoint’s height −3.

questions.independentReasoning: After the horizontal input shift, sequences x=1±h sample f at 3±h. The two corresponding plotted segment endpoint heights are both 4. Their point-value assignment at exactly 3 is not sampled by the limiting sequence.
optionReview: Correct: as x approaches 1, the input x+2 to f approaches 3, where the nearby graph height approaches 4.
This substitutes the isolated value f(3) for its nearby limiting behavior.
This is the approached input to f, not f’s approached output.
This is the approached input to g and does not give its output.

optionReview: At x=0 the left and right heights are 1 and 2, so the sides disagree.
